messages:
mike: seeing a sudden batch of ALB target deregistrations in eu-west-1 edge pool starting ~10:40 UTC. targets removed with healthcheck timeout even though pods show Ready. rolling back a change now but want quick triage. :eyes:

ashok: any recent kube-proxy / cni changes on those nodes?

mike: no kube-proxy rollout, we did a small systemd-resolved restart on nodes (to pick up certs) around 10:38. suspecting DNS oddness but ALB healthchecks hit IPs, right?

sara: can you paste one of the ALB healthcheck logs + a curl from node to pod?

mike: pasted snippets below. note the ALB shows repeated HTTP/1.1 504 from target; from the node the probe endpoint responds quickly.

```
ALB: healthcheck failure: 10.0.45.12:8080 GET /health -> 504 timed out after 5s
node# tcpdump: 10.0.45.12 <- 34.198.12.45: healthcheck SYN, no ACK
```

```
mike@edge-node:~$ curl -sv --max-time 2 http://10.0.45.12:8080/health
* Connected to 10.0.45.12 (10.0.45.12) port 8080 (#0)
> GET /health HTTP/1.1
> Host: 10.0.45.12
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< content-type: application/json
{ "ok": true }
```

ashok: interesting — ALB can't complete handshake but node->pod works. Could be SNAT/egress ephemeral port exhaustion on node or conntrack entries preventing ALB->node flow. Also seen iptables DNAT rules that changed after systemd-resolved restart when kube-proxy reloaded.

olivia: @mike can you check conntrack counters on the node and `iptables -t nat -L -n -v` ? If nat table is missing or has stale rules ALB might be hitting the node ENI but packets silently dropped.

mike: conntrack shows high ESTABLISHED count but not full. nat table looks ok, but I see a weird rule in PREROUTING rewriting healthcheck Host header -> old pod IP: `DNAT tcp -- 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.0.0/8 tcp dpt:8080 to:10.0.50.99:8080` and that pod IP (10.0.50.99) doesn't exist anymore. systemd-resolved restart coincided with kubelet re-resolving service DNS -> kube-proxy applied a stale mapping?

sara: that maps to stale DNS->endpoint caching on node. ALB hit node:8080, iptables forwarded to dead pod IP, so no ACK to ALB -> timeout -> deregister.

ingress-oncall: quick mitigation: 1) increase ALB healthcheck unhealthy threshold / timeout temporarily to avoid cascading deregistrations, 2) roll restart kube-proxy on affected nodes to rebuild nat rules, 3) run `conntrack -L | grep 10.0.50.99` and delete stale entries.

mike: doing 1 and 2 now. bumping healthcheck timeout to 10s and unhealthy threshold to 5. restarting kube-proxy on 3 nodes (one at a time). will post results. :thumbsup:

ci-bot: config-change: ALB target-group tg-rt-edge-eu update healthcheck timeout=10s unhealthy_threshold=5 by mike@infra (change-id: cfg-20260318-11)

ashok: also file a follow-up to avoid systemd-resolved restarts coinciding with kube-proxy reload. we should ensure kube-proxy watches for DNS changes without rewriting NAT rules to stale endpoints. possible fixes: disable DNS-based endpoint mapping on node, or use `EndpointSlices` + ipvs mode to avoid DNAT to pod IPs.

mike: after kube-proxy restart, ALB healthchecks passed for two nodes. one more node finishing. deleting stale conntrack entries removed the DNAT forwarding to dead pod IPs. looks stable so far.

olivia: opened infra ticket INF-1123 to track root cause and action items (preventive): avoid systemd-resolved restarts during maintenance windows, add probe path Host header check, and add a short grace period in ALB target deregistration automation.

mike: thumbs up. will run a small job to scan nodes for DNAT rules pointing to non-existent pod IPs and alert. thanks everyone. :tada:
